newsitem.title: HAITI: Ex-FRAPH leader criticizes foreign troops in Haiti.
newsitem.headline: Ex-FRAPH leader criticizes foreign troops in Haiti.

text.p: The fugitive former leader of a Haitian military group said in a radio interview on Thursday that international troops and organisations were to blame for political divisions in Haiti.

Jodel Chamblain, who was second in command of the Front for the Advancement and Progress for Haiti (FRAPH) and was wanted for human rights abuses, made his comments in a telephone interview, apparently from within Haiti.
He is wanted by Haitian authorities in connection with thousands of deaths and human rights violations committed after the bloody 1991 coup that ousted former President Jean-Bertrand Aristide.
"Foreign management...is what is causing division in this country," Chamblain told Radio Metropole.
"The moment has come to return to nationalism to create any real model of democracy."
Chamblain, who fled to the Dominican Republic at the time of the 1994 U.S. military intervention, told Radio Metropole he recently returned to Haiti.
About 20,000 U.S. troops restored Aristide to power in 1994 after he spent three years in exile.

The U.S. troops were replaced by United Nations peacekeepers, whose current mandate ends on July 31. The U.N. mission has been extended several times due to insecurity and the inability of the Haitian National Police force to maintain order.
At least 50 people in the town of Gonaive, about 40 miles (64 km) north of Port-au-Prince, blocked roads on Wednesday to voice their opposition to an extension of the U.N. mission.

The Movement for the National Reconstruction, a coalition of grassroots groups, accused the U.N. mission of creating insecurity to justify its presence in Haiti. U.N. officials said it was a small demonstration and did not comment further.
Chamblain was principal deputy to Emmanuel "Toto" Constant in running FRAPH.

Constant is also wanted by Haitian authorities for his role in human rights abuses during the years that Aristide was in exile. He lives in Queens, New York, a borough of New York City. The U.S. government has refused extradition requests, saying his presence would destabilise Haiti further.
